title: Awe and time
hook: a study found awe made people feel they had more time (Rudd, Vohs and Aaker)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the awe walk: fresh eyes, the vast and the small, and a smaller self in the photos. Your line was awe walk. Today, what awe might do to the clock.

How much time do you have right now? Not on the clock. In your body. Some days the answer is none at all: the inbox, the pickup, the dinner, the thing you promised. Minutes feel like coins falling through a hole in a pocket. Seneca, the Roman philosopher, wrote to a friend that time was the only thing truly ours, and that we let it slip away anyway. Centuries later, a team of researchers tried something odd. Instead of teaching people to manage time, they showed them something vast, then asked about the clock.
screen: `HOW MUCH TIME DO YOU HAVE?` → `COINS THROUGH A HOLE.` → `SHOW THEM SOMETHING VAST.`

segments.voice: The researchers were Melanie Rudd, Kathleen Vohs and Jennifer Aaker. First, the setup. They brought people into a feeling of awe, for example with a video of vast, astonishing scenes, or by having them recall or read about a moment of awe. Others were brought into ordinary happiness, or a neutral mood. Then everyone answered questions about time. Second, the finding in the paper's title: awe expanded people's sense of time. The awe group felt they had more time available, and felt less impatient. Not more hours on the clock; a wider feeling of the hours they had. Third, what came with it. The awe group was more willing to give their time to help others, and leaned toward spending on experiences rather than things. Awe seemed to loosen people's grip on their minutes. Fourth, why that might make sense. The researchers suggested that awe pulls a person into the present moment, and the present, fully noticed, seems to hold more. Seneca had already said what's at stake. In Richard Gummere's translation of his first letter: "Nothing, Lucilius, is ours, except time." The study adds a strange, hopeful twist. The way to more time may not be squeezing the day harder. It may be stopping, for a moment, in front of something bigger than the day.
screen: `AWE, HAPPINESS, OR NEUTRAL.` · `MORE TIME, LESS IMPATIENCE.` · `MORE WILLING TO GIVE TIME AWAY.` · `THE PRESENT HOLDS MORE.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS OURS, EXCEPT TIME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something vast, the ocean, a canyon, a night full of stars, or a view you've actually stood in front of, and stay with it without checking the time. Each time a task drifts in, notice it and go back to the vast thing, letting each breath out run a little longer. At the end, just notice whether the next hour looks any different from here.
Melanie Rudd. Lead researcher of a study where people brought into awe reported feeling they had more time, and less impatience. Today's word.
Your line: more time. Not more hours, a wider feeling of the ones you have. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who use awe this way pause in a rushed moment to look at something vast, such as the sky, the sea, or a wide view, and let their attention settle on the present before going back to the day.
